escape noise and work – fresh air – slow life

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a quiet place that I would love to visit, which is Mai Chau Valley in Hoa Binh Province. It's about three hours from Hanoi.

I know about it from my colleague. He posted beautiful photos on Facebook, with green rice fields, mountains and old wooden houses. Since then, I have wanted to go there.

If I went there, I would sleep late, walk around the villages, ride a bike through the rice fields, and try local food. I'd also bring a book to read.

I would like to go with my family, because my parents and my brother are always busy, and we rarely travel together.

I want to go because my life in Hanoi is noisy and stressful. A quiet place with fresh air would help me relax and slow down.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a quiet place I'm dying to visit: Mai Chau Valley in Hoa Binh Province, about three hours from Hanoi.

I first heard about it from a colleague who posted stunning photos on Facebook: green rice fields, misty mountains and traditional stilt houses. I've been meaning to go ever since.

If I got the chance, I'd sleep in, wander through the villages, cycle along the paddy fields and try the local specialities. I'd also bring a book to read on the balcony.

I'd love to go with my family, because we're all so busy that we hardly ever travel together.

The main reason is that I'm craving a break from the noise and pressure of city life. A peaceful place with fresh air would let me slow down and recharge my batteries.
grammar: **Điều kiện loại 2** → "If I **got** the chance, I **'d sleep** in."
**Mệnh đề quan hệ "who"** → "a colleague **who** posted photos."
**so + adj + that** → "so busy that we hardly ever travel."
**Present perfect + ever since** → "I've been meaning to go ever since."

p3.q: Why do people like going to quiet places?
p3.a6: Quiet places help people relax and forget stress. They can think clearly and sleep better there. Modern life is noisy, so people need some peace.
p3.a7: Because they offer relief from stress and noise. In quiet surroundings people can think clearly, unwind and recharge, which is a welcome contrast to hectic modern life.

p3.q: What kinds of places are usually quiet?
p3.a6: Libraries, parks in the early morning, villages, mountains and temples are usually quiet. Some cafés are quiet too.
p3.a7: Libraries, rural villages, mountain areas, temples and parks early in the morning, basically anywhere far from traffic and crowds.

p3.q: Do people nowadays have enough opportunities to enjoy peace and quiet?
p3.a6: I don't think so. People work long hours and live in crowded cities. Even at home, they hear noise from the street or from their phones.
p3.a7: Not really. Long working hours, crowded cities and constant phone notifications leave little room for real peace and quiet, even at home.

p3.q: Why is it difficult for people to find quiet places in cities?
p3.a6: Cities have heavy traffic, construction and many people. Land is expensive, so there are few parks. Most areas are busy and loud.
p3.a7: Traffic, construction and dense populations create constant noise, and because land is so expensive, green spaces are rare and quiet corners are quickly built over.

p3.q: Do young people prefer quiet places or lively places?
p3.a6: Most young people prefer lively places because they like meeting friends and having fun. But some, like me, enjoy quiet places to relax after work.
p3.a7: Generally lively ones, since they want to socialise and have fun. That said, more young people nowadays, myself included, appreciate quiet spots to switch off after a stressful week.

p3.q: Is it important for children to spend time in quiet places?
p3.a6: Yes, it is. Quiet time helps children focus, read and use their imagination. But they also need to play and make noise.
p3.a7: Yes, it helps them concentrate, develop their imagination and learn to be comfortable alone. Of course, they also need plenty of active play, so a balance is ideal.

p3vocab.m: sự giải tỏa khỏi; *hectic* = bận rộn hối hả.
xa giao thông; *rural* = nông thôn.
thông báo; *leave little room for* = còn ít chỗ cho.
dân cư đông đúc; *built over* = bị xây lên.
tắt đầu óc nghỉ ngơi; *socialise* = giao lưu.
trí tưởng tượng; *a balance* = sự cân bằng.

cards.title: Describe a long trip that you often take but do not like
points: why you often have to make this trip
and explain why you do not like it
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: chuyến đi là về quê bà ở Thanh Hóa bằng xe khách (khoảng 4 giờ), mỗi dịp Tết và giỗ. Bạn bị say xe nên không thích. Khớp với bà ở quê (đề 18). Bạn thay bằng chuyến đi thật.

notes.v: grandmother's village – Thanh Hoa
coach from My Dinh – sometimes with family
4 hours (6 hours at Tet) – traffic
Tet – death anniversaries – visit grandma
motion sickness – crowded – bad road – back pain – tired

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a long trip that I often take but don't like. It's the trip from Hanoi to my grandmother's village in Thanh Hoa Province.

I usually go by coach from My Dinh bus station. Sometimes I travel with my parents, and sometimes I go alone. The trip normally takes about four hours, but during Tet it can take six hours because of heavy traffic.

I have to make this trip several times a year. I go home for Tet, for family death anniversaries, and also when my grandmother is not well.

I don't like it because I get carsick easily, so I feel dizzy and tired. The coach is often crowded, the seats are narrow, and the road is bumpy, so I get a backache. Although I don't like the journey, I love seeing my grandmother, so I never miss it.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a long trip I make regularly but can't say I enjoy: the journey from Hanoi to my grandmother's village in Thanh Hoa Province.

I normally take a coach from My Dinh bus station, sometimes with my parents and sometimes on my own. It usually takes about four hours, but around Tet it can stretch to six because of the heavy traffic.

I have to make this trip several times a year: for Tet, for family death anniversaries and whenever my grandmother is unwell.

What I dislike is that I'm prone to motion sickness, so I'm often dizzy and nauseous by the end. On top of that, the coaches tend to be packed, the seats are cramped and the road is bumpy, which leaves me with a sore back. Still, seeing my grandmother makes it all worthwhile, so I wouldn't dream of missing it.
grammar: **can't say I + V** → "can't say I enjoy" (nói giảm).
**whenever + mệnh đề** → "whenever my grandmother is unwell."
**leave + O + with + N** → "leaves me with a sore back."
**wouldn't dream of + V-ing** → nhấn mạnh.

p3.q: Why do people dislike long journeys?
p3.a6: They are tiring and boring, and people have to sit for a long time. Some people get carsick, and traffic jams make it worse.
p3.a7: They're tiring and tedious: sitting for hours in cramped seats, battling traffic and, for some, motion sickness. It's time that feels wasted.

p3.q: What are the most common reasons people make long trips?
p3.a6: Most people travel for work, for holidays or to visit family. Some people also travel to study in other cities.
p3.a7: Business, holidays and family visits are the main ones, particularly around Tet in Vietnam, when millions of people head back to their hometowns.

p3.q: Do people prefer travelling by car, train or plane for long journeys?
p3.a6: It depends. Planes are fast but expensive, trains are comfortable, and cars or coaches are cheaper and go door to door. In Vietnam many people choose coaches because they are cheap.
p3.a7: It depends on budget and distance. Planes are fastest but pricey, trains are comfortable, and coaches or cars are flexible and affordable, which is why coaches remain so popular in Vietnam.

p3.q: What can people do to make a long journey more enjoyable?
p3.a6: They can listen to music, watch films, read or talk with friends. It also helps to bring snacks and a pillow, and to take breaks.
p3.a7: Entertainment helps: music, podcasts or films. Bringing snacks, a neck pillow and travelling with good company make a big difference, as do regular rest stops.

p3.q: Why do some people enjoy travelling while others do not?
p3.a6: Some people like new places and new experiences. Others prefer a comfortable routine, and they worry about cost, safety or getting tired.
p3.a7: It comes down to personality: adventurous people crave new experiences, while others value comfort and routine and find travel stressful or costly.

p3.q: Do you think travelling by public transport will become more popular in the future?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Traffic and pollution are getting worse, and the government is building more metro lines. Public transport is also cheaper.
p3.a7: Probably, yes. With worsening congestion and pollution, and new metro lines opening in Hanoi, more people will see public transport as a practical, cheaper alternative.

p3vocab.m: tẻ nhạt; *battle traffic* = vật lộn với giao thông.
quay về; *hometown* = quê.
đến tận nơi; *affordable* = giá phải chăng.
gối cổ; *rest stop* = trạm nghỉ.
thích phiêu lưu; *it comes down to* = tùy thuộc vào.
ùn tắc; *a practical alternative* = lựa chọn thay thế thiết thực.

cards.title: Describe a party that was held after a special event
points: what you did at the party
and explain why you remember this party
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: sự kiện đặc biệt là dự án của team bạn go-live thành công; sau đó cả team 12 người ăn tiệc nướng tối hôm đó. Rất hợp đời sống IT. Bạn thay bằng tiệc thật (sau đám cưới, tốt nghiệp...).

notes.v: big project went live – 6 months
BBQ restaurant near company
12 team members + manager
ate – toasts – games – speeches – bonus
hard work – relief – team closer – manager's speech

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a party after a very important event at my company. The event was the launch of a big project that my team had worked on for six months.

The party was held at a barbecue restaurant near our office, on the same evening that the project went live. All twelve members of the team came, together with our manager.

We ate a lot of grilled meat, took photos and drank to our success. Our manager gave a short speech to thank everybody, and we played some funny games.

I remember this party because we had worked very hard, and sometimes we even worked at weekends. So when the project finally succeeded, we all felt relieved and happy. The party also made our team closer. It's one of my best memories at work.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a party held after a major milestone at my company: the launch of a big project that my team had been working on for six months.

The party took place at a barbecue restaurant near our office, on the very evening the project went live. All twelve members of the team came, along with our manager.

We tucked into plenty of grilled meat, took lots of photos and raised our glasses to our success. Our manager gave a short speech to thank everyone for their efforts, and we played a few silly games to wind down.

It's a party I'll always remember because we had put in months of hard work, including a few weekends. So when the project finally went smoothly, we were all hugely relieved and proud. The evening also brought the team closer together, and I still count it among my best memories at work.
grammar: **Quá khứ hoàn thành** → "my team **had been working** on for six months."
**Bị động** → "The party **was held** at..."
**so + mệnh đề** → "So when it succeeded, we felt relieved."
**along with / together with** → "along with our manager."

p3.q: Why do people like having parties after special events?
p3.a6: To celebrate and share their happiness with others. Parties also help people relax after hard work and make friends closer.
p3.a7: It's a way to mark the occasion and share the joy with others. Parties also let people unwind after a stressful period and strengthen their bonds.

p3.q: What kinds of events do people usually celebrate with a party?
p3.a6: Weddings, birthdays, graduations, new jobs and company successes. In Vietnam, Tet and house-warming parties are also important.
p3.a7: Weddings, birthdays, graduations and promotions, as well as holidays such as Tet. In Vietnam, house-warming parties are popular too.

p3.q: Do people prefer large parties or small gatherings?
p3.a6: It depends. Young people often like big parties for fun, but many people prefer small gatherings with close friends because they can talk more.
p3.a7: It varies. Large parties are lively, but I prefer small gatherings, where you can have proper conversations with the people you're close to.

p3.q: What makes a party enjoyable?
p3.a6: Good food, nice music and good friends. The atmosphere should be relaxed, and the host should take care of the guests.
p3.a7: Good company, tasty food, music that suits the crowd and a relaxed atmosphere. A thoughtful host makes everyone feel welcome.

p3.q: Why are some people reluctant to attend parties?
p3.a6: Some people are shy or introverted, so they feel uncomfortable with many people. Others are too tired or don't like noise or drinking.
p3.a7: Introverts often find big social events draining, and others dislike the noise, the pressure to drink or simply feel exhausted after work.

p3.q: Do you think people spend too much money on parties?
p3.a6: Sometimes, yes. In Vietnam, weddings can be very expensive because people invite hundreds of guests. I think it's better to spend less and save money for the future.
p3.a7: In some cases, yes. Vietnamese weddings, for example, can cost a fortune, with hundreds of guests. I think a simpler celebration and more savings would be wiser.

p3vocab.m: đánh dấu dịp đặc biệt; *strengthen bonds* = thắt chặt gắn kết.
thăng chức; *house-warming* = tân gia.
buổi tụ họp; *proper conversation* = cuộc trò chuyện đúng nghĩa.
không khí; *thoughtful host* = chủ tiệc chu đáo.
người hướng nội; *draining* = làm kiệt sức.
tốn cả gia tài; *wiser* = khôn ngoan hơn.

cards.title: Describe a change that you made recently
points: what you did for the change
and explain how you feel about the change
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: thay đổi là giảm dùng điện thoại trước khi ngủ, ngủ sớm lúc 11 giờ và đọc sách (nối với đề 22). Bạn thay bằng thay đổi thật (tập gym, dậy sớm, làm skincare...).

notes.v: stop using phone before bed – sleep by 11 – read
scrolling till 1 a.m. – tired – dark circles – skin bad
phone charge outside bedroom – alarm clock – book – skincare routine
more energetic – better skin – focus at work – proud

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a change I made recently in my daily routine. I stopped using my phone before going to bed, and now I go to sleep at eleven o'clock.

The reason was that I used to scroll through videos until one o'clock in the morning. I was always tired at work, and I had dark circles under my eyes. I care about my appearance, so that really worried me.

To change this habit, I charge my phone outside my bedroom and use an alarm clock instead. Before bed, I read a book for about twenty minutes and do my skincare routine.

I feel very good about this change. I wake up with more energy, my skin looks better, and I can focus more at work. I'm proud of myself because it wasn't easy to give up the habit.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a change I made recently to my daily routine: I've stopped using my phone in bed, and I now aim to be asleep by eleven.

What prompted it was that I used to scroll through videos until one in the morning. I was constantly tired at work and had dark circles under my eyes, which bothered me, as I care about how I look.

To break the habit, I now charge my phone outside the bedroom and use an old-fashioned alarm clock. Before bed, I read for about twenty minutes and go through my skincare routine.

I'm really pleased with the result. I wake up feeling refreshed, my skin looks healthier and I can concentrate much better at work. I'm proud of myself, too, because kicking a habit like that was harder than I'd expected.
grammar: **used to + V** → "I used to scroll..."
**Present perfect** → "I've stopped using my phone."
**Mệnh đề quan hệ chỉ cả câu** → "..., **which** bothered me."
**harder than I'd expected** → so sánh + quá khứ hoàn thành.

p3.q: Is it easier for young people to change?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Young people are more open to new things and have fewer fixed habits. They also learn faster.
p3.a7: Generally, yes. Young people are more adaptable, have fewer ingrained habits and are less afraid of trying new things.

p3.q: Is it easy for old people to change?
p3.a6: Not really. They have lived with their habits for many years, so it's hard to change. They also feel more comfortable with what they know.
p3.a7: Not usually. Their habits are deeply set after decades, and many are more comfortable with the familiar. That said, with encouragement, some adapt well.

p3.q: How can people change their daily routine if they want to?
p3.a6: They should start with small steps, such as waking up ten minutes earlier. They can write a plan and ask a friend to remind them. It's important to be patient.
p3.a7: Start small: wake up fifteen minutes earlier, for instance, rather than overhauling everything at once. Writing a plan, tracking progress and having a friend hold you accountable all help.

p3.q: What are the disadvantages when people keep making changes?
p3.a6: They may feel unstable and stressed. They can also waste time and money, and others may not trust them if they change their plans too often.
p3.a7: Constant change can be unsettling and stressful, and people may never stick with anything long enough to see results. It can also cost time and money, and weaken trust at work.

p3vocab.m: dễ thích nghi; *ingrained* = ăn sâu.
ăn sâu; *the familiar* = điều quen thuộc.
thay đổi toàn bộ; *hold someone accountable* = giám sát ai.
gây bất ổn; *stick with* = kiên trì với.

cards.title: Describe a time when you changed an important opinion of yours
points: and explain how you felt about the experience
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: ý kiến cũ là "làm Tester không cần giỏi tiếng Anh"; thay đổi sau khi phải đọc tài liệu và viết bug report tiếng Anh với khách nước ngoài (nối với đề 5, quyết định học IELTS). Bạn thay bằng chuyện thật.

notes.v: two years ago – first foreign client project
testers don't need English – Vietnamese enough
English docs – unclear bug reports – misunderstanding – missed chances
embarrassed – then motivated – started learning

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time when I changed an important opinion. It was about two years ago, when my company started a project for a foreign client.

Before that, I believed that software testers didn't need good English. I thought Vietnamese was enough, because we mostly worked with Vietnamese colleagues.

But on that project, I had to read documents in English and write bug reports for the client. My English was not good, so my reports were sometimes unclear, and the client misunderstood me. Because of this, we wasted time, and I also missed some chances to join important meetings.

I felt embarrassed at first, but then I understood that English is very important for my career. This was the reason why I decided to study for IELTS. Now I'm happy that I changed my mind.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a time when I completely changed my mind about something important. It happened about two years ago, when my company took on a project for a foreign client.

Until then, I'd always believed that software testers didn't need good English. Since we mostly worked with Vietnamese colleagues, I assumed Vietnamese would be enough.

On that project, though, I had to read English documentation and write bug reports for the client. My English was weak, so my reports were sometimes unclear and the client misunderstood me. That led to wasted time, and I also missed out on a few meetings that would have been good for my career.

I felt rather embarrassed at first, but it was a real wake-up call. I realised that English is a key skill in IT, and that's what pushed me to start studying for IELTS. I'm glad I changed my mind, even though it took a mistake to make me see it.
grammar: **Quá khứ hoàn thành** → "I'd always believed..."
**Since + lý do** → "Since we mostly worked with Vietnamese colleagues."
**would have + V3** → "meetings that would have been good."
**that's what + V** → "that's what pushed me to..."

p3.q: Why do people change their opinions?
p3.a6: Because they get new information or new experiences. Sometimes they listen to other people or learn from their mistakes.
p3.a7: Usually because of new information or first-hand experience, as in my case. Others change their views after being exposed to different perspectives.

p3.q: Is it easy for people to admit they were wrong?
p3.a6: No, it isn't. Many people feel embarrassed or worry about losing face. In Vietnam, "face" is very important, so it's harder.
p3.a7: Not at all. Pride and fear of losing face get in the way, particularly in cultures like ours where saving face matters a great deal.

p3.q: Do older people change their opinions less often than young people?
p3.a6: Yes, usually. They have more life experience and strong habits, so they are more stubborn. Young people are more flexible.
p3.a7: Generally, yes. Their views have been shaped by decades of experience, so they tend to be set in their ways, whereas young people are more open-minded.

p3.q: Can other people influence our opinions? How?
p3.a6: Yes, they can. Family, friends, teachers and social media all influence us. For example, a friend's advice may change how we see something.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Family, friends and colleagues shape our views through advice and example, and social media and influencers now play a huge part too.

p3.q: Is it important to listen to different viewpoints?
p3.a6: Yes, it is. We can learn new things and understand other people better. It also helps us make better decisions.
p3.a7: Yes, it broadens our horizons, helps us see problems from other angles and leads to better-informed decisions.

p3.q: Should people always stick to their own opinions?
p3.a6: No. If you are wrong, you should change. But if you are sure about your values, you should not change just because others say so.
p3.a7: Not necessarily. We should hold firm on our core values but stay flexible on matters where better evidence emerges.

p3vocab.m: trải nghiệm trực tiếp; *be exposed to* = được tiếp xúc với.
mất mặt; *get in the way* = cản trở.
khó thay đổi; *open-minded* = cởi mở.
định hình quan điểm; *influencer* = người có ảnh hưởng.
mở rộng tầm nhìn; *viewpoint* = quan điểm.
giá trị cốt lõi; *hold firm* = giữ vững.

cards.title: Describe a law on environmental protection
points: how you first learned about it
and explain how you feel about this law
cards.note: Lưu ý quan trọng 1: Part 3 của đề này trong PDF bị lệch chủ đề (hỏi về luật lệ trường học ở Trung Quốc, có vẻ chép nhầm). Mình giữ 6 câu của PDF (Q1–Q6, trả lời theo trường học ở Việt Nam) và thêm 2 câu bonus (Q7–Q8) bám sát chủ đề môi trường.

notes.v: rule on sorting household waste at source
apartment notice / news on TV / company talk
everyone – cleaner city – workers – future generations – recycling
support – good idea – needs time to get used to – more bins needed

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a law on environmental protection, which is the rule about sorting household waste. It says that people must separate their rubbish into different groups, for example food waste, recyclable waste and other waste.

I first learned about it from the news on TV, and then from a notice in my neighbourhood.

I think many people benefit from this law. A cleaner city is better for everyone. Rubbish workers also have an easier job, and the recycling companies can reuse more materials. In the long term, future generations will have a healthier environment.

I really support this law. At first, it was a little inconvenient because I had to prepare different bins at home. But now it has become a habit. I think we need more rubbish bins in public places so that people can follow it more easily.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about an environmental protection law that requires households to sort their rubbish at source, separating food waste, recyclables and general waste.

I first heard about it on the TV news, and later saw a notice about it in my neighbourhood.

The benefits are wide-ranging. Residents get a cleaner city, waste collectors have an easier job, and recycling companies can recover far more material. In the long run, it also eases the burden on landfills, which benefits future generations.

I'm fully behind the law. It was a bit of a hassle at first, because I had to set up separate bins at home, but it has gradually become second nature. That said, I think more clearly labelled bins are needed in public places, otherwise it's hard for people to comply.
grammar: **Mệnh đề quan hệ "that"** → "a law **that** requires households..."
**Present perfect** → "it has gradually become second nature."
**otherwise + mệnh đề** → "otherwise it's hard to comply."
**That said,...** → nhượng bộ.

p3.q: What kinds of rules do schools in China have? (trả lời theo Việt Nam)
p3.a6: I don't know about China, but in Vietnamese schools students must wear uniforms, arrive on time, respect teachers and not use phones in class. They also have to keep the school clean.
p3.a7: I can't speak for China, but in Vietnam, students are expected to wear uniforms, be punctual, respect teachers and avoid using phones in class. Keeping the school clean is part of the rules too.

p3.q: Do you think school rules are important?
p3.a6: Yes, I do. Rules keep order and teach students discipline. Without rules, the school would be chaotic and unsafe.
p3.a7: Yes, they maintain order and instil discipline. Without them, schools would be chaotic and some students would be unable to learn.

p3.q: Are children unhappy with the school rules?
p3.a6: Some are, especially about strict rules like hair length or no phones. But many understand the reasons for the rules.
p3.a7: Some are, particularly with strict rules about hair or phones, but most come to accept them once they understand the reasoning.

p3.q: How can parents help their children understand and follow rules?
p3.a6: Parents should explain the reasons calmly and be a good example. They can praise children when they follow rules.
p3.a7: By explaining the reasons patiently, leading by example and praising good behaviour rather than only punishing bad.

p3.q: What are the rules people should obey at work?
p3.a6: People should arrive on time, respect colleagues, follow safety rules and keep company information secret. They should also meet deadlines.
p3.a7: Be punctual, treat colleagues with respect, follow safety procedures, protect confidential information and meet deadlines.

p3.q: What is the purpose of punishment?
p3.a6: To stop people from breaking rules and to teach them to behave better. Fear of punishment also keeps society safe.
p3.a7: Mainly deterrence: it discourages people from breaking rules, and it can teach offenders to behave better and protect society.

p3.q: Do you think laws can solve environmental problems?
p3.a6: Laws help, but they are not enough. People also need to be educated. The government must also check and punish people who break the rules.
p3.a7: Laws are a vital first step, but they only work with enforcement and public awareness. Without education, people simply look for ways around the rules.

p3.q: Who should take more responsibility for protecting the environment, the government or individuals?
p3.a6: Both. The government makes laws and builds facilities, and individuals change their habits, like sorting rubbish. Companies should also take responsibility.
p3.a7: Both. Governments set rules and provide infrastructure, companies must reduce their waste, and individuals have to change daily habits such as sorting rubbish.

p3vocab.m: đúng giờ; *uniform* = đồng phục.
rèn kỷ luật; *chaotic* = hỗn loạn.
nghiêm khắc; *reasoning* = lý do.
làm gương; *good behaviour* = hành vi tốt.
thông tin mật; *meet deadlines* = đúng hạn.
sự răn đe; *offender* = người vi phạm.
thực thi; *public awareness* = nhận thức cộng đồng.

p3.q: What kinds of ambitions do people have?
p3.a6: Some want to have a successful career or get high positions. Some want to run their own business, travel the world or have a happy family.
p3.a7: They vary widely: career success, starting a business, financial security, travelling the world or simply raising a happy family.

p3.q: Why should parents encourage children to have ambitions?
p3.a6: Ambitions give children motivation and a direction in life. They also make children work harder and feel more confident.
p3.a7: Ambitions give children direction and motivation, and teach them to work towards something meaningful, which builds confidence and resilience.

p3.q: Should parents interfere with children's ambitions?
p3.a6: I think parents should give advice, but not force their children. Children should choose their own dreams, but parents can help them understand the risks.
p3.a7: Parents should guide rather than dictate. They can offer advice and highlight risks, but the final decision should belong to the children.

p3.q: Is there any difference between children's ambitions and those of grown-ups?
p3.a6: Yes. Children's dreams are often big and imaginative, like being an astronaut. Adults' goals are more realistic and often about money, job and family.
p3.a7: Definitely. Children dream big and imaginatively, whereas adults' goals tend to be more practical and tied to career, money and family responsibilities.

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time when I sent a message to my old university friend, Nam, but he didn't reply for a long time.

I sent him a message on Zalo about a class reunion. I asked if he could come, and I told him the date and place. I really wanted him to come because he was one of my closest friends at university.

cards.a7:

I'd sent him a message on Zalo about a class reunion, asking whether he could make it and giving him the date and venue. I was keen for him to come, since he'd been one of my closest friends at university.

To my surprise, there was no response. I waited two days, then three, and still nothing. I even tried calling him, but nobody picked up.

p3.q: Do you think children are born smart or they learn to become smart?
p3.a6: I think both are true. Some children are born with a good brain, but learning and a good environment are more important. Hard work can make any child smarter.
p3.a7: It's a mix of nature and nurture. Some children may have a natural aptitude, but a supportive environment and sustained effort matter far more.

p3.q: How do children become smarter at school?
p3.a6: They learn from teachers, read books and do homework. They also learn from friends and by taking part in activities.
p3.a7: Through good teaching, reading, regular practice and group activities that develop critical thinking and teamwork.

p3.q: Why are some people well-rounded and others only good at one thing?
p3.a6: It depends on interests and opportunities. Some people try many things from childhood, while others focus on only one thing. Time and family support also matter.
p3.a7: It comes down to interests, opportunities and upbringing. Some are encouraged to explore widely, while others specialise early to excel in one field.

p3.q: Why does modern society need talents of all kinds?
p3.a6: Society has many jobs, like doctors, engineers and artists. Each kind of talent is useful, so we need many types of people to work together.
p3.a7: Modern society is complex, requiring engineers, doctors, artists and many more. Diverse talents complement each other and drive progress.

p3.q: Do people reply to messages more quickly these days than in the past?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Almost everyone has a smartphone, so people expect fast answers. But some people still reply late because they are busy.
p3.a7: Generally yes. With smartphones in everyone's pocket, instant replies have become the norm, though some people still take ages when they're busy.

p3.q: Why do some people not reply to messages?
p3.a6: They may be busy, forget, or not know what to say. Some people also feel stressed by too many messages.
p3.a7: They may be swamped with work, simply forget, or feel overwhelmed by constant notifications. Occasionally, it's a deliberate way of avoiding someone.

p3.q: Is it rude not to reply to a message?
p3.a6: It depends. For work messages, it's rude because others are waiting. For casual chats, it's fine to reply later, but a short reply is polite.
p3.a7: It depends on the context. Ignoring work messages is unprofessional, whereas with casual chats a delayed reply is understandable, though a quick acknowledgement is courteous.

p3vocab.m: bẩm sinh và nuôi dưỡng; *aptitude* = năng khiếu.

toàn diện; *specialise* = chuyên sâu.

p3.q: Why do children enjoy stories about animals?
p3.a6: Animals are cute and funny, and children love them. Animals in stories can talk and act like people, so children find them interesting and easy to understand.
p3.a7: Animals are cute and relatable, and the fact that they talk and act like people makes the stories fun and easy to follow.

p3.q: What can people learn from animal stories?
p3.a6: They can learn moral lessons, like being kind, honest and brave. They can also learn about nature and how to treat animals.
p3.a7: Moral lessons such as honesty, kindness and courage, delivered in a gentle way, along with a greater respect for nature and wildlife.

p3.q: Do films influence how people view animals?
p3.a6: Yes, they do. Films can make people love animals like lions or pandas. But sometimes they show wrong images, for example, sharks as only dangerous.
p3.a7: Very much. Films can foster affection for animals, but they can also distort perceptions, for instance by portraying sharks purely as killers.

p3.q: Why are animals often used in stories?
p3.a6: Writers use animals to show human behaviour in a simple way. It's also safer to criticise bad behaviour through animals. Animals also attract children.
p3.a7: Animals let authors illustrate human qualities in a simple, non-threatening way, and they appeal strongly to children, which makes the lessons stick.

p3.q: Should children learn about animals at school?
p3.a6: Yes, they should. They can learn about nature and how to protect animals. School trips to the zoo can also be very interesting.
p3.a7: Yes, it fosters curiosity about the natural world and teaches responsibility towards living things. Field trips to zoos or wildlife parks make it far more memorable.

p3.q: Do people care more about animal welfare nowadays?
p3.a6: I think so. Many people now adopt pets instead of buying them and support groups that protect wild animals. Social media also spreads information fast.
p3.a7: Yes, awareness has grown noticeably. More people adopt rather than buy pets, and social media quickly spotlights cruelty cases, putting pressure on authorities to act.

p3.q: Why do companies use celebrities in advertisements?
p3.a6: Celebrities attract attention because many people like them. Fans also trust them and want to be like them, so they buy the product.
p3.a7: Celebrities grab attention instantly, and fans often trust and want to emulate them, so the brand's image benefits from the association.

p3.q: Do celebrity advertisements influence consumers?
p3.a6: Yes, especially young people and fans. They may buy a product just because their idol uses it. But people who are careful will also check reviews.
p3.a7: Certainly, particularly among younger fans, who may buy a product simply because their idol endorses it. More cautious shoppers, though, compare reviews first.

p3.q: Are advertisements more creative nowadays?
p3.a6: Yes. Now they use short videos, funny stories and social media challenges. They are more interesting than the old ads on TV.
p3.a7: Generally, yes. Brands now rely on short videos, humour and viral social media challenges, which are far more engaging than the old-style TV commercials.

p3.q: What makes an advertisement effective?
p3.a6: It should be short, clear and easy to remember. A good song or story helps. It also needs to show the real benefit of the product.
p3.a7: A clear message, a memorable tune or slogan and an emotional story that sticks in people's minds, as well as a realistic demonstration of the product's benefits.

p3.q: Do children get influenced by advertisements easily?
p3.a6: Yes, they do. Children can't tell the difference between advertising and real information. They want toys and snacks they see in ads.
p3.a7: Very easily. Children often can't distinguish between persuasion and information, so they pester their parents for whatever they see advertised.

p3.q: Should there be stricter control of advertising?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Some ads give false information or are bad for children, for example ads for fast food or alcohol. The government should check them more carefully.
p3.a7: I think so. Misleading claims and ads aimed at children, such as for junk food, call for tighter regulation and heavier fines for false advertising.

cards.title: Describe a place you have travelled to that you would like to recommend to others

cards.note: Thông tin giả định: nơi trong bài là Ninh Bình (Tràng An, Tam Cốc), cách Hà Nội khoảng 2 giờ, bạn đi cùng bạn bè. Phần Part 3 PDF chỉ có 3 câu, mình thêm 2 câu bonus. Bạn thay bằng nơi thật.

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about Ninh Binh, a place that I would like to recommend to everyone. It's a province about two hours south of Hanoi.

I went there last year with my friends for a weekend trip. We took a small boat trip through the caves at Trang An, and the scenery was amazing, with tall limestone mountains and green water. After that, we climbed hundreds of steps to the top of Hang Mua and enjoyed the view of the rice fields. In the evening, we tried the local specialty, which is goat meat.

I recommend it for three reasons. First, it's very beautiful. Second, it's close to Hanoi and not expensive. Third, it's good for people who like both nature and culture, because there are also old temples. I think it's best to go on a weekday, because it's less crowded.

I went there last year with some friends for a weekend trip. We took a boat ride through the caves at Trang An, where the scenery was breathtaking, with towering limestone mountains and emerald water. Afterwards, we climbed hundreds of steps up Hang Mua for a panoramic view of the rice fields. In the evening, we tried the local speciality, goat meat.

I'd recommend it for several reasons. For one thing, it's stunningly beautiful. For another, it's close to Hanoi and very affordable, so it makes a perfect weekend getaway. p3.q: Is it important to take photos while travelling?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Photos help us remember the trip and share it with friends and family. But we shouldn't spend too much time on the phone and forget to enjoy the place.
p3.a7: To a degree. Photos are lovely keepsakes and a way to share the trip, but if people are glued to their phones they miss the moment itself, so a balance is best.

p3.q: Can you trust other people's travel journals on the Internet?
p3.a6: Not completely. Some people exaggerate or get paid to write good things. I usually read many reviews and compare them before I decide.
p3.a7: Not blindly. Some reviews are exaggerated or sponsored, so I cross-check several sources and look for recent, detailed reviews with real photos.

p3.q: What factors affect how people feel about travel?
p3.a6: The weather, the cost, the food and the people they travel with all matter. Transport problems or a bad hotel can also spoil the trip.
p3.a7: Many things: weather, budget, accommodation, food and, above all, the company. Transport hiccups or a poor hotel can spoil an otherwise lovely trip.

p3.q: Why do many people like to travel on holiday?
p3.a6: They want to relax, see new places and try new food. Travel is also a break from work and a chance to spend time with family.
p3.a7: To unwind, experience new cultures and cuisines, and escape the daily grind. It's also a precious chance to bond with family and friends.

p3.q: Do you think tourism is always good for a place?
p3.a6: Not always. It brings money and jobs, but too many tourists can cause rubbish and traffic, and damage nature. Local people must protect their place.
p3.a7: Not always. It generates income and jobs, but overtourism can cause litter, congestion and damage to natural sites, so tourism needs to be managed sustainably.

and explain how you solved it
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: vấn đề là môi trường test (test server) bị sập ngay trước ngày release, cả team không test được; bạn cùng dev tìm ra lỗi cấu hình. Hợp nghề IT Tester của bạn. Bạn thay bằng chuyện thật.

notes.v: test server crashed – couldn't open the system
day before release – at the office – evening
deadline – whole team stuck – manager worried – no clear cause
checked logs – found wrong setting – asked developer – fixed – re-tested

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a technological problem that I faced at work. It was the day before an important release, and our test server suddenly crashed.

It happened at the office in the afternoon. When I tried to open the system, I only saw an error message. Nobody in the team could test anything, and our manager was very worried because the deadline was the next day.

It was very challenging because I didn't know the cause, and we had very little time. First, I checked the log files and found a wrong setting after an update. Then I asked a developer for help, and we fixed it together. After that, I tested the system again, and everything worked.

I felt tired but also proud, because we finished on time. I learned that I should stay calm and check the logs first.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a technical problem I ran into at work: the day before an important release, our test server suddenly went down.

It happened in the office one afternoon. When I tried to open the system, all I got was an error message. Nobody on the team could test anything, and our manager was on edge because the deadline was the next day.

It was a real challenge, since the cause wasn't obvious and we were up against the clock. I started by going through the log files, and I spotted a wrong setting that had been introduced in a recent update. I then asked a developer to help me, and together we corrected it. Finally, I re-ran the tests to make sure everything worked.

I was exhausted, but also proud that we delivered on time. The experience taught me to keep a cool head and to check the logs before panicking.

**since + lý do** → "since the cause wasn't obvious."

p3.q: What kinds of technological problems do people often face?
p3.a6: Slow internet, broken phones or computers, forgotten passwords and software errors. Sometimes people also lose data or get viruses.
p3.a7: Everyday ones such as unstable internet, software glitches, forgotten passwords and device failures, and more serious ones like data loss and cyberattacks.

p3.q: How has technology made people's lives easier?
p3.a6: We can communicate quickly, shop online and work from home. Technology also saves time, for example, using apps to pay bills or call a taxi.
p3.a7: It has transformed communication, shopping, banking and work. A task that once took hours, like paying bills, now takes seconds on a phone.

p3.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Many people can't live without their phones. They use maps for every trip and calculators for easy sums. When technology fails, they feel lost.
p3.a7: I believe so. Many of us are lost without our phones, relying on them for directions, memory and even basic maths, which leaves us helpless when technology fails.

p3.q: What should people do when technology fails?
p3.a6: They should stay calm, restart the device and check the connection. If it doesn't work, they should ask for help from an expert. It's also good to have a backup plan.
p3.a7: Stay calm, try basic fixes such as restarting, then seek expert help if needed. It's wise to have backups of important data and an offline plan.

p3.q: Will technology become more reliable in the future?
p3.a6: I think so. Engineers learn from mistakes and make better systems. Artificial intelligence can also find errors faster. But no technology is perfect.
p3.a7: Probably. Engineers keep learning from failures, and AI can detect faults earlier. That said, no system is ever completely flawless.

cards.title: Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages
points: how you got to know him/her
how he/she learns a new language
and explain how you feel about him/her
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: người trong bài là bạn đại học tên Trang, nói được tiếng Anh, tiếng Hàn và một ít tiếng Nhật; học bằng app, xem phim và nói theo (shadowing). Bạn thay bằng người thật. Đây cũng là đề có thể nhắc lại hành trình học IELTS của bạn.

notes.v: Trang – university – same English club
apps – Korean dramas – shadowing – notebook – practises 30 min daily
English, Korean, some Japanese
admire – inspired – a bit jealous – want to ask for tips

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my friend Trang, who is very good at learning languages. I got to know her at university, because we were both members of the English club.

She has her own way of learning. She uses language apps every day, watches Korean dramas, and repeats the actors' sentences to practise pronunciation. She also writes new words in a small notebook, and she practises for thirty minutes every day, even when she's busy.

She can speak English and Korean very well, and she also speaks some Japanese.

I really admire her. She works hard and never gives up. She inspires me to study English more seriously, and sometimes I feel a little jealous. I often ask her for advice about how to learn better.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my friend Trang, who has a real gift for languages. I met her at university, where we were both in the English club.

She has a very effective routine. She uses language apps daily, watches Korean dramas and repeats the actors' lines to improve her pronunciation, a technique known as shadowing. She also jots down new words in a small notebook and sticks to thirty minutes of practice every day, however busy she is.

She speaks English and Korean fluently, and she can get by in Japanese too.

I truly admire her. She's disciplined and persistent, and she's inspired me to take my own English more seriously. I'll admit I'm a little envious sometimes, but mostly I'm grateful, because she's always happy to share her study tips with me.

grammar: **Mệnh đề quan hệ "who"** → "my friend Trang, **who** has a real gift."
**however + adj + S + V** → "however busy she is."
**Present perfect** → "she's inspired me."

p3.q: At what age should children start learning a foreign language?
p3.a6: I think the earlier the better, maybe from five or six years old. Young children learn pronunciation more naturally. But learning should be fun, like songs and games, not too much pressure.
p3.a7: The earlier the better, ideally from around five or six, since young children pick up pronunciation effortlessly. It should be playful, though, through songs and games, rather than pressured.

p3.q: Which skill is more important, speaking or writing?
p3.a6: I think speaking is more important in daily life because we use it to communicate every day. But writing is also important for work and exams, like emails and reports.
p3.a7: For most people, speaking, as we communicate verbally far more often. That said, writing is essential at work, where emails and reports matter, so ideally both.

p3.q: Does a person still need to learn other languages if he or she is good at English?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Another language can open new job chances and help us understand other cultures. English is not enough in every country.
p3.a7: Yes. A second foreign language opens up career opportunities, deepens cultural understanding and is a real asset, because English alone doesn't suffice everywhere.

p3.q: Do you think minority languages will disappear?
p3.a6: Some of them may disappear, because young people use bigger languages like English or Vietnamese for work and study. But if the government and communities teach them at school, they can be saved.
p3.a7: Some are at risk, as younger generations gravitate towards dominant languages for jobs and education. With support, such as teaching them in schools and recording them, many can be preserved.

bằng lời nói; *essential* = thiết yếu.

cards.title: Describe a food that people eat on special occasions/events
points: and explain why people eat it on that special occasion/event

notes.v: Tet (Lunar New Year) – banh chung
glutinous rice – mung beans – pork – dong leaves – wrap – boil 8–10 hours
tradition – symbol of earth – gratitude to ancestors – family reunion

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about "banh chung", a traditional food that Vietnamese people eat at Tet, the Lunar New Year.

It's a square cake. It's made from sticky rice, mung beans and fatty pork, and it's wrapped in green leaves called "la dong". First, we wash the rice and beans and put them in the leaves with the pork. Then we wrap them tightly into a square shape and tie them with string. After that, we boil the cakes for eight to ten hours. In my family, my grandmother and my mother make them together, and the whole family sits around the pot at night.

People eat banh chung at Tet for several reasons. It's a tradition from a long time ago. The square shape is a symbol of the earth. It also shows respect to our ancestors, and making it brings the family together.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about "banh chung", a traditional dish that Vietnamese people eat at Tet, the Lunar New Year.

It's a square cake made from sticky rice, mung beans and fatty pork, wrapped in green "dong" leaves. To make it, we first wash the rice and beans, then layer them with the pork inside the leaves. We wrap everything tightly into a square, tie it with string and boil the cakes for eight to ten hours. In my family, my grandmother and mother make them together, and the whole family gathers around the pot at night, chatting and keeping the fire going.

People eat it at Tet for a few reasons. It's a time-honoured tradition, and the square shape symbolises the earth. It's also a way of paying respect to our ancestors, and the process of making it brings the family closer together, which is really what Tet is about.

**First... Then... After that...** → trình tự các bước.
**Mệnh đề quan hệ "that"** → "a dish **that** Vietnamese people eat."
**which is really what Tet is about** → mệnh đề quan hệ chỉ cả câu.

p3.q: Which food is generally popular in your country?
p3.a6: Pho is probably the most popular, and also banh mi, bun cha and spring rolls. They are delicious and cheap, and foreign visitors like them too.
p3.a7: Pho is arguably the best known, along with banh mi, bun cha and spring rolls. They're tasty, affordable and increasingly popular with tourists.

p3.q: Do families still cook traditional food for festivals?
p3.a6: Yes, many families still do, especially in the countryside. But in cities, some people buy ready-made food because they are busy.
p3.a7: Many do, particularly in rural areas. In cities, though, busy families increasingly buy ready-made versions for convenience.

p3.q: Why is food important in celebrations?
p3.a6: Food brings people together. Sharing a meal is a way to show love and respect. Special dishes also remind people of their culture.
p3.a7: Food is the heart of most celebrations: sharing a meal strengthens family ties, expresses love and keeps cultural traditions alive.

p3.q: Are young people interested in traditional dishes?
p3.a6: Some are not, because they prefer fast food or foreign food. But many still love traditional dishes at Tet because they remember their childhood.
p3.a7: Mixed. Many prefer fast food, but at Tet, nostalgia for childhood flavours draws most of them back to traditional dishes.

cards.title: Describe a live sports event you watched and liked
points: when and where you watched it

cards.note: Thông tin giả định: sự kiện là một trận bóng đá của đội tuyển Việt Nam, bạn xem trực tiếp trên màn hình lớn ở quán cà phê cùng đồng nghiệp (không nêu tên giải hay tỉ số để bạn thay bằng trận thật). Part 3 PDF chỉ có 3 câu, mình thêm 2 câu bonus.

notes.v: football match – Vietnam national team
last year – evening – café with big screen
colleagues – 10 people

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a live football match of the Vietnam national team that I watched and really liked.

I watched it last year in the evening at a café near my company, which had a big screen. I went there with about ten colleagues from my company. We all wore red T-shirts and some people brought small flags.

I liked it for several reasons. First, the match was very exciting. Vietnam scored a goal in the last minutes, and everybody in the café jumped up and shouted. Second, the atmosphere was great. We cheered together, sang songs and hugged each other. I'm not a big sports fan, but that night I felt very proud of my country.

After the match, we walked home with many people in the street, and everyone was happy. It's an unforgettable evening for me.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a live football match featuring the Vietnam national team that I watched and thoroughly enjoyed.

I watched it last year one evening at a café near my office with a big screen. About ten colleagues and I went together, and we all wore red T-shirts, with some of us waving small flags.

There were a couple of reasons I loved it. For one thing, the match was nail-biting: Vietnam scored in the final minutes, and the whole café erupted, jumping up and cheering. For another, the atmosphere was electric. We sang, chanted and hugged strangers. I'm not a big sports fan, but that night I felt immensely proud of my country.

p3.q: What kinds of sports events are broadcast on TV or other media in your country?
p3.a6: Football is the most popular. People also watch badminton, volleyball and the SEA Games. Now many matches are also live on YouTube or apps.
p3.a7: Football dominates, followed by badminton, volleyball and multi-sport events like the SEA Games. These days, many matches are also streamed live on YouTube and apps.

p3.q: Do people in your country enjoy watching football games?
p3.a6: Yes, very much. Football is like a passion for many Vietnamese people. When the national team plays, people gather in cafés or stay at home to watch, and the streets are crowded after a win.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Football is a national passion: when the national team plays, cafés fill up, families huddle around the TV and the streets erupt after a win.

p3.q: Does encouragement and applause from the audience have an impact on athletes?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Support makes them feel confident and gives them more energy, especially at home matches. But too much pressure can also make some players nervous.
p3.a7: Definitely. A supportive crowd boosts confidence and energy, which is why home advantage matters, though the same pressure can unsettle some players.

p3.q: Is it better to watch sports live at the stadium or on TV?
p3.a6: The stadium has a better atmosphere, but tickets are expensive and it's far. TV is cheaper and more comfortable, and you can see replays.
p3.a7: The stadium offers an unbeatable atmosphere, but tickets and travel are costly. TV is cheaper, comfortable and offers replays, so I'm happy with the screen.

p3.q: Why do some people prefer to play sports rather than watch them?
p3.a6: Playing is good for health and helps people make friends. Watching is relaxing, but it doesn't keep you fit.
p3.a7: Because playing keeps you fit, relieves stress and builds friendships, whereas watching is passive. I should exercise more myself, to be honest.

cards.title: Describe a person you know who would like to choose a career in the medical field
points: when he/she started to think about that
what he/she would like to do

cards.note: Thông tin giả định: người trong bài là em trai của bạn, học lớp 11, muốn làm bác sĩ sau khi thấy bà ốm nằm viện (nối đề 29). Bạn thay bằng người thật.

notes.v: my younger brother – 17 – since he was born

become a doctor – study medicine – work in hospital – children

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my younger brother, who wants to work in the medical field. He's seventeen years old and in grade eleven, and I have known him since he was born.

He started thinking about it last year, when our grandmother was in the hospital for two weeks. He went to visit her every day and saw how kind and hard-working the doctors and nurses were.

Now he would like to study medicine at a university and become a doctor. He wants to work in a hospital, and perhaps he will treat children.

I think he wants this career for several reasons. First, he wants to help people who are sick. Second, doctors are respected in our society, and the job is stable. He studies very hard, especially biology and chemistry. I'm proud of him, and I hope he can achieve his dream.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my younger brother, who's set his heart on a career in medicine. He's seventeen, in grade eleven, and I've known him all his life, obviously.

The idea first occurred to him last year, when our grandmother spent two weeks in hospital. He visited her every day and was deeply impressed by how kind and dedicated the doctors and nurses were.

He now hopes to study medicine at university and become a doctor, perhaps working with children in a hospital.

There are a couple of reasons behind his choice. For one thing, he genuinely wants to help people who are suffering. For another, doctors are highly respected in our society, and the job offers stability. He's been working hard, especially in biology and chemistry. I'm very proud of him, and I really hope he gets in.

**would like to + V** → "he would like to study medicine."
**Present perfect continuous** → "He's been working hard."

p3.q: Why do some people choose to work in the medical field?
p3.a6: Many want to help others and save lives. The job is respected and stable, and the salary can be good. Some choose it because their family members are doctors.
p3.a7: Mostly out of a desire to help people and save lives. The profession also offers respect, job security and a decent income, and some follow in the footsteps of family members.

p3.q: How does working in a medical-related profession impact a person's life?
p3.a6: Doctors and nurses work long hours and often have night shifts, so they have less time for their families. The job is also stressful. But they feel happy when patients get better.
p3.a7: It's demanding: long hours, night shifts and high stress leave little time for family. On the flip side, seeing patients recover is deeply rewarding.

p3.q: Do you think medical professionals are valued in society?
p3.a6: In Vietnam, yes, they are respected, especially doctors. But I think nurses deserve more respect and a better salary. During COVID, many people appreciated them more.
p3.a7: Generally yes, doctors in particular. I'd argue, though, that nurses deserve more recognition and better pay, something the pandemic made far more obvious.

p3.q: In your opinion, which profession is more important: doctors or nurses?
p3.a6: I think both are equally important. Doctors diagnose and treat the disease, and nurses take care of the patients every day. They need to work as a team.
p3.a7: Both are indispensable. Doctors diagnose and prescribe treatment, while nurses provide day-to-day care, and neither can work effectively without the other.

p3.q: How can technology influence medical-related professions in the future?
p3.a6: AI can help doctors find diseases faster. Robots can help with operations, and patients can see doctors online. This will save time and reduce mistakes.
p3.a7: AI will help detect diseases earlier, robots will assist in surgery, and telemedicine will let patients consult doctors remotely, cutting costs and reducing errors.

p3.q: What qualities are essential for someone to succeed in a medical profession?
p3.a6: They need to be patient, kind and responsible. They also need to be strong because the job is hard. Good knowledge and teamwork skills are important too.
p3.a7: Compassion, patience, a strong sense of responsibility and resilience under pressure, together with solid knowledge and good teamwork.

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a time when I worked in a group at university. It was in my final year, for our graduation project.

There were five people in my group, and our leader was my friend Hung. Our task was to build a small mobile app, and we had three months to do it.

My role was the tester. I wrote test cases, looked for bugs, and told the developers to fix them. I also helped to prepare the presentation.

At first, I felt stressed because we had many arguments about the ideas and the schedule. But our leader listened to everybody, and we made a clear plan. I learned a lot about teamwork, and my English was also better because we read English documents. In the end, we got a good mark, and I felt very proud of the group.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a time when I worked in a group at university, on our graduation project in the final year.

There were five of us, led by my friend Hung. Our task was to build a small mobile app within three months.

My role was tester: I wrote test cases, hunted down bugs and reported them to the developers, and I also helped prepare the presentation.

To begin with, it was quite stressful, because we kept disagreeing over ideas and deadlines. But Hung was good at listening to everyone, and together we drew up a clear plan, which made things run much more smoothly. p3.q: How do people in a team usually view their leader?
p3.a6: It depends on the leader. If he is fair and listens to others, people respect him. If he is bossy or lazy, people don't like him. In my group, everyone liked Hung because he was kind and fair.
p3.a7: It depends on the leader's style. Fair, approachable leaders earn respect, whereas bossy or disorganised ones lose it quickly. In my group, Hung was well liked because he was fair and a good listener.

p3.q: What do you think are the characteristics of a good leader?
p3.a6: A good leader should be responsible and fair. He should listen to others, communicate clearly and make decisions at the right time. He should also be a good example for the team.
p3.a7: Responsibility, fairness, clear communication and the ability to make timely decisions. A good leader also listens, motivates the team and leads by example.

p3.q: What happens if you don't have a good leader?
p3.a6: The team may be confused and have many arguments. Nobody knows what to do, so the work is late and the quality is low. Good members may also leave.
p3.a7: The team lacks direction, so conflicts arise, deadlines slip and quality suffers, and talented members may eventually leave.

p3.q: Why do some people not like teamwork?
p3.a6: Some people prefer working alone because they can work at their own speed. Others don't like arguments, or they worry that some members don't work hard but still get the credit.
p3.a7: Some prefer working independently at their own pace, dislike conflicts, or resent "free riders" who do little but share the credit.

p3.q: Do you think young people are suitable for teamwork?
p3.a6: Yes, I think so. Young people are energetic, open to new ideas and good with technology. But some of them are too individual, so they need to learn to cooperate.
p3.a7: Generally, yes. They're energetic, open-minded and tech-savvy, although some need to learn to put the team before themselves.

lost office job – loved skincare – small online shop, Facebook, TikTok live
skincare – imported – honest advice
trust – good service – real reviews – now 5 staff – a small shop

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a woman called Mai, who has a successful business. She's thirty-two years old and she used to be my neighbour.

I got to know her many years ago, and now I'm one of her customers because I like to buy skincare products from her.

She started her business three years ago. She lost her office job, but she was interested in skincare, so she decided to open a small online shop. At first, she sold products on Facebook, and later she sold on TikTok live streams.

Her service is very good, and she answers every message. Because of this, customers trust her, and they come back. Now she has five staff and a small shop in Hanoi.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about Mai, a woman I know who runs a very successful business. She's thirty-two and used to be my neighbour.

I've known her for years, and these days I'm also one of her customers, since I buy my skincare products from her.

She set up the business three years ago. She'd just lost her office job and had always been passionate about skincare, so she decided to open a small online shop. She started out selling on Facebook, then moved on to live-streaming on TikTok.

Her shop specialises in imported skincare products. I think she's successful for a few reasons. For one thing, she gives honest advice and never pushes products people don't need. p3.q: Would you like to start a family business?
p3.a6: Maybe in the future. I would like to work with my family because we trust each other. But it can be difficult if we argue. Now I want to gain more experience at a company first.
p3.a7: Possibly one day. I like the idea of working with people I trust, but mixing family and business can be tricky. For now, I'd rather gain experience at a company first.

p3.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of family businesses?
p3.a6: The advantages are trust, flexibility and strong support. The disadvantages are that family conflicts can affect the business, and it may be hard to separate work and family life.
p3.a7: On the plus side, there's mutual trust, flexibility and strong commitment. On the downside, family disputes can spill over into the business, and it's hard to switch off from work at home.

p3.q: What qualities do people need to run a successful business?
p3.a6: They need to be hard-working, patient and willing to learn. They should also understand customers and manage money well.
p3.a7: Perseverance, adaptability, a good grasp of customers' needs and sound financial management, plus the courage to take calculated risks.

p3.q: Why do many small businesses fail?
p3.a6: Many don't have enough money or experience. Some don't understand the market, and competition is strong, so they can't make a profit.
p3.a7: Typically due to a lack of capital and experience, poor market research and fierce competition, so they never become profitable.

p3.q: Has the Internet changed the way people do business?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. People can open shops online without a large amount of money and sell to customers in many places. Social media is also an easy way to advertise.
p3.a7: Enormously. It has lowered the barrier to entry, letting people launch shops cheaply and reach customers nationwide, with social media as a low-cost marketing channel, exactly as Mai did.

p3vocab.m: rắc rối; *gain experience* = tích lũy kinh nghiệm.
lan sang; *commitment* = sự tận tâm.
khả năng thích nghi; *calculated risk* = rủi ro có tính toán.
vốn; *fierce competition* = cạnh tranh khốc liệt.

cards.title: Describe a person who loves to grow plants (e.g. vegetables, flowers) at home or in the garden
points: and explain why he/she loves growing plants
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: người trong bài là mẹ của bạn, trồng rau thơm và hoa trên sân thượng của căn nhà ba tầng (khớp thông tin nhà ở ngoại thành). Part 3 của PDF có 4 câu; mình thêm 3 câu về trồng cây/thực phẩm vốn bị đặt nhầm ở đề 41. Bạn thay bằng người thật.

notes.v: my mother – 50s – housewife / part-time
herbs (mint, basil), morning glory, chilli, roses, orchids
roof terrace – foam boxes – compost – water twice a day – talks to plants
clean food – relaxing hobby – pleasure to see growth – gives gifts to neighbours

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about my mother, who loves growing plants. She's in her fifties, and she spends most of her free time on the roof of our house.

She grows vegetables and flowers. For vegetables, she grows herbs like mint and basil, water spinach and chilli. For flowers, she has some roses and orchids.

She grows them in foam boxes and big pots on the roof terrace. She uses kitchen waste to make compost, and she waters the plants twice a day. I often hear her talking to the plants, which makes me laugh.

I think she loves growing plants because the vegetables are clean and safe for the family. It also helps her relax after housework. She feels very happy when she sees the plants grow, and she often gives vegetables to our neighbours. I really appreciate her hobby.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about my mother, who's passionate about growing plants. She's in her fifties and spends most of her spare time on the roof terrace of our house.

She grows both vegetables and flowers. On the vegetable side, there are herbs such as mint and basil, water spinach and chillies, and she also has a few roses and orchids.

She plants them in foam boxes and large pots. She makes her own compost out of kitchen waste and waters everything twice a day. I sometimes overhear her chatting to the plants, which always makes me smile.

The reasons she loves it are quite simple. For one thing, the vegetables are fresh and chemical-free, so she knows the family is eating safely. For another, it helps her unwind after housework, and she gets a real sense of satisfaction from watching things grow. She often shares the harvest with the neighbours, too. I really admire her dedication.
grammar: **Mệnh đề quan hệ "who"** → "my mother, **who's** passionate..."
**both... and...** → "both vegetables and flowers."
**make + O + V** → "which makes me smile."
**out of + N** → "compost out of kitchen waste."

p3.q: What do you think of the job of a farmer?
p3.a6: It's a hard but important job. Farmers work outdoors in the hot sun and the rain, and their income is not high. But without them, we have no food, so they should be respected.
p3.a7: It's gruelling but vital. Farmers work long hours in all weather for modest incomes, yet society depends on them for food, so they deserve far more respect and support.

p3.q: Are there many people growing their own vegetables now?
p3.a6: Yes, more and more people do, even in the city. Many people grow them on balconies or roofs because they worry about food safety.
p3.a7: Increasingly so, even in cities, where people use balconies and rooftops, largely out of concern for food safety.

p3.q: Do you think it's good to let kids learn how to plant?
p3.a6: Yes, it is. Children learn about nature and responsibility, and they enjoy eating vegetables they grew. It also keeps them away from screens.
p3.a7: Definitely. It teaches them patience, responsibility and where food comes from, and it gets them away from screens.

p3.q: What are the differences between traditional and modern agriculture?
p3.a6: Traditional farming uses a lot of human work and simple tools. Modern farming uses machines, technology and chemicals, so it produces more food, but it can pollute the environment.
p3.a7: Traditional agriculture is labour-intensive and relies on simple tools, whereas modern agriculture uses machinery, technology and fertilisers to boost yields, though sometimes at an environmental cost.

p3.q: Do Vietnamese people grow plants?
p3.a6: Yes, very much. Vietnam is an agricultural country, and many families in the countryside grow rice and vegetables. Even in cities, people grow flowers for Tet.
p3.a7: Very much so. Vietnam has a strong agricultural tradition, and even city dwellers grow herbs and flowers, especially for Tet.

p3.q: Why do some people prefer planting food themselves?
p3.a6: They want clean and safe food without chemicals. It's also cheaper and a relaxing hobby, and the vegetables are fresh.
p3.a7: To be sure the food is chemical-free, to save money and because gardening is therapeutic. Home-grown produce is also fresher.

p3.q: Will there be more and more people planting food in the future?
p3.a6: I think so. People care more about health, and new methods like growing in small boxes or on walls make it easy for city people.
p3.a7: I think so. With growing health awareness, and techniques like vertical gardening making it feasible in small urban spaces, more people will take it up.

p3vocab.m: vất vả; *modest income* = thu nhập khiêm tốn.
an toàn thực phẩm; *rooftop* = sân thượng.
nguồn gốc thực phẩm; *patience* = kiên nhẫn.
tốn nhiều sức người; *yield* = sản lượng.
thuộc nông nghiệp; *city dweller* = cư dân thành phố.
giúp thư giãn; *produce* = nông sản.
vườn thẳng đứng; *feasible* = khả thi.

cards.title: Describe an interesting video
points: when and where you watched it
and explain how you feel about it
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: video là vlog du lịch Hà Giang trên YouTube, bạn xem trên xe bus đi làm. Part 3 PDF có 3 câu, mình thêm 2 câu bonus. Bạn thay bằng video thật.

notes.v: last month – on the bus to work – phone
travel vlog – Ha Giang Loop – motorbike – mountains – local people
recommended by YouTube – wanted to relax – bus trip is long
amazed – want to go – inspired to save money

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about an interesting video that I watched last month. It was a travel vlog about the Ha Giang Loop in the north of Vietnam.

I watched it on my phone on the bus to work in the morning. My trip to the office takes about one hour, so I usually watch videos to pass the time.

The video is about a group of young people who travel around Ha Giang by motorbike for four days. They go through high mountains, small villages and beautiful roads. They also meet local people and try local food.

I watched it because YouTube recommended it to me, and I wanted something relaxing. I felt amazed by the beautiful views, and I really want to go there. After that video, I started saving some money for a trip next year.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about an interesting video I watched last month: a travel vlog about the Ha Giang Loop in northern Vietnam.

I watched it on my phone during my morning bus ride to work. My commute takes about an hour, so I usually watch videos to pass the time.

The video follows a group of young people riding around Ha Giang for four days, passing through towering mountains, tiny villages and spectacular winding roads. Along the way, they meet local people and sample regional dishes.

I watched it because YouTube recommended it, and I was in the mood for something relaxing. I was absolutely amazed by the scenery, and it made me want to go there myself. In fact, it motivated me to start saving for a trip next year.

p3.q: What kinds of things are popular on social media?
p3.a6: Short videos, funny clips, music, news and beauty tips are popular. Food and travel videos are also very popular in Vietnam.
p3.a7: Short-form videos, memes, music, celebrity gossip, and lifestyle content such as food, travel and beauty tips.

p3.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using social media?
p3.a6: It helps us keep in touch, share information and learn new things. But it wastes time, and fake news and bad comments can also hurt people.
p3.a7: It keeps us connected and informed, and creates business opportunities. On the downside, it's addictive, spreads misinformation and exposes people to cyberbullying.

p3.q: What do you think of making friends on social networks?
p3.a6: It can be good, because we can meet people who share the same interests. But it can be unsafe, because some people lie about who they are. We should be careful.
p3.a7: It can be rewarding, as you meet like-minded people, but there are risks, since people may not be who they claim to be, so caution is essential.

p3.q: Do you prefer watching videos or reading articles?
p3.a6: I prefer videos, because they are easier to understand and more fun. But for study, I think reading is better because I can go at my own speed.
p3.a7: For entertainment, videos, since they're engaging and effortless. For learning, I prefer articles, where I can set my own pace and revisit details.

p3.q: Can people learn useful things from videos?
p3.a6: Yes, a lot. There are videos about cooking, English and computer skills. I also watch English videos to improve my listening.
p3.a7: Absolutely. Tutorials on cooking, languages and coding are a goldmine, and I watch English videos to sharpen my listening.

gây nghiện; *misinformation* = thông tin sai lệch.
cùng chí hướng; *caution* = sự thận trọng.
không tốn sức; *revisit* = xem lại.
kho báu; *sharpen* = trau dồi.

cards.title: Describe a tall building you like or dislike
points: and explain why you like/dislike it
cards.note: Thông tin giả định: tòa nhà là Keangnam Hanoi Landmark Tower (Nam Từ Liêm, Hà Nội), dùng làm văn phòng, căn hộ và trung tâm thương mại. Bạn nên tự kiểm tra lại số tầng/chức năng nếu muốn nói chính xác. Part 3 PDF chỉ hỏi về chỗ ở, mình thêm 2 câu bonus về nhà cao tầng. Bạn thay bằng tòa nhà thật.

notes.v: offices, apartments, shopping mall
Nam Tu Liem – west Hanoi – my bus passes by
glass, tall, over 70 floors, two towers – modern – lights at night
landmark – modern – proud – view from the top

cards.a6:
I'd like to talk about a tall building that I like. It's the Keangnam Landmark Tower in Hanoi.

It's used for several purposes. There are offices, apartments and a shopping centre inside. It's in the west of Hanoi, in Nam Tu Liem District, and my bus passes by it every day.

It looks very modern. It's a very tall glass building with more than seventy floors, and it has a few towers. At night, it's covered with lights, so it looks beautiful.

I like it for two reasons. First, it's a landmark of Hanoi, and I can see it from far away, even from my neighbourhood. Second, it reminds me that my city is developing quickly, and I feel proud of this. I've never been to the top, but I would like to go there one day to enjoy the view.
cards.a7:
I'd like to talk about a tall building that I really like: Keangnam Landmark Tower in Hanoi.

It's a mixed-use building, housing offices, apartments and a shopping centre. It's located in Nam Tu Liem District in the west of the city, and my bus goes past it every day.

It's strikingly modern: a huge glass skyscraper with over seventy floors, made up of several towers. At night it's lit up, which makes it look spectacular.

I like it for a couple of reasons. For one thing, it's a real landmark: I can spot it from miles away, even from my neighbourhood. For another, it symbolises how fast Hanoi is developing, which makes me feel proud. I haven't been to the top yet, but I'd love to go one day and take in the view over the city.
